presentation: CHIEF COMPLAINT: , Newly diagnosed high-risk acute lymphoblastic leukemia; extensive deep vein thrombosis, right iliac vein and inferior vena cava (IVC), status post balloon angioplasty, and mechanical and pharmacologic thrombolysis following placement of a vena caval filter.,HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: , The patient was transferred here the evening of 02/23/2007 from Hospital with a new diagnosis of high-risk acute lymphoblastic leukemia based on confirmation by flow cytometry of peripheral blood lymphoblasts that afternoon.  History related to this illness probably dates back to October of 2006 when he had onset of swelling and discomfort in the left testicle with what he described as a residual "lump" posteriorly.  The left testicle has continued to be painful off and on since.  In early November, he developed pain in the posterior part of his upper right leg, which he initially thought was related to skateboarding and muscle strain.  Physical therapy was prescribed and the discomfort temporarily improved.  In December, he noted onset of increasing fatigue.  He used to work out regularly, lifting lifts, doing abdominal exercises, and playing basketball and found he did not have energy to pursue these activities.  He has lost 10 pounds since December and feels his appetite has decreased.  Night sweats and cough began in December, for which he was treated with a course of Augmentin.  However, both of these problems have continued.  He also began taking Accutane for persistent acne in December (this agent was stopped on 02/19/2007).  Despite increasing fatigue and lethargy, he continues his studies at University of Denver, has a biology major (he aspires to be an ophthalmologist).,The morning of 02/19/2007, he awakened with severe right inguinal and right lower quadrant pain.  He was seen in Emergency Room where it was noted that he had an elevated WBC of 18,000.  CT scan of the abdomen was obtained to rule out possible appendicitis and on that CT, a large clot in the inferior vena cava extending to the right iliac and femoral veins was found.  He promptly underwent appropriate treatment in interventional radiology with the above-noted angioplasty and placement of a vena caval filter followed by mechanical and pharmacologic thrombolysis.  Repeat ultrasound there on 02/20/2007 showed no evidence of deep venous thrombosis (DVT).  Continuous intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion was continued.  Because there was no obvious cause of this extensive thrombosis, occult malignancy was suspected.  Appropriate blood studies were obtained and he underwent a PET/CT scan as part of his diagnostic evaluation.  This study showed moderately increased diffuse bone marrow metabolic activity.  Because the WBC continued to rise and showed a preponderance of lymphocytes, the smear was reviewed by pathologist, Sheryl Asplund, M.D., and flow cytometry was performed on the peripheral blood.  These studies became available the afternoon of 02/23/2007, and confirmed the diagnosis of precursor-B acute lymphoblastic leukemia.  The patient was transferred here after stopping of the continuous infusion heparin and receiving a dose of Lovenox 60 mg subcutaneously for further diagnostic evaluation and management of the acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).,ALLERGIES: , NO KNOWN DRUG ALLERGIES.  HE DOES SEEM TO REACT TO CERTAIN ADHESIVES.,CURRENT MEDICATIONS:  ,1.  Lovenox 60 mg subcutaneously q.12h. initiated.,2.  Coumadin 5 mg p.o., was administered on 02/19/2007 and 02/22/2007.,3.  Protonix 40 mg intravenous (IV) daily.,4.  Vicodin p.r.n.,5.  Levaquin 750 mg IV on 02/23/2007.,IMMUNIZATIONS: , Up-to-date.,PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:  ,The treatment of the thrombosis as noted above on 02/19/2007 and 02/20/2007.,FAMILY HISTORY:  ,Two half-brothers, ages 26 and 28, both in good health.  Parents are in good health.  A maternal great-grandmother had a deep venous thrombosis (DVT) of leg in her 40s.  A maternal great-uncle developed leukemia around age 50.  A maternal great-grandfather had bone cancer around age 80.  His paternal grandfather died of colon cancer at age 73, which he had had since age 68.  Adult-onset diabetes is present in distant relatives on both sides.,SOCIAL HISTORY:  ,The patient is a student at the University majoring in biology.  He lives in a dorm there.  His parents live in Breckenridge.  He admits to having smoked marijuana off and on with friends and drinking beer off and on as well.,REVIEW OF SYSTEMS: , He has had emesis off and on related to Vicodin and constipation since 02/19/2007, also related to pain medication.  He has had acne for about two years, which he describes as mild to moderate.  He denied shortness of breath, chest pain, hemoptysis, dyspnea, headaches, joint pains, rashes, except where he has had dressings applied, and extremity pain except for the right leg pain noted above.,PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:  ,GENERAL:  Alert, cooperative, moderately ill-appearing young man.,VITAL SIGNS:  At the time of admission, pulse was 94, respirations 20, blood pressure 120/62, temperature 98.7, height 171.5 cm, weight 63.04 kg, and pulse oximetry on room air 95%.,HAIR AND SKIN:  Mild facial acne.,HEENT:  Extraocular muscles (EOMs) intact.  Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation (PERRLA), fundi normal.,CARDIOVASCULAR:  A 2/6 systolic ejection murmur (SEM), regular sinus rhythm (RSR).,LUNGS:  Clear to auscultation with an occasional productive cough.,ABDOMEN:  Soft with mild lower quadrant tenderness, right more so than left; liver and spleen each decreased 4 cm below their respective costal margins.,MUSCULOSKELETAL:  Mild swelling of the dorsal aspect of the right foot and distal right leg.  Mild tenderness over the prior catheter entrance site in the right popliteal fossa and mild tenderness over the right medial upper thigh.,GENITOURINARY:  Testicle exam disclosed no firm swelling with mild nondiscrete fullness in the posterior left testicle.,NEUROLOGIC:  Exam showed him to be oriented x4.  Normal fundi, intact cranial nerves II through XII with downgoing toes, symmetric muscle strength, and decreased patellar deep tendon reflexes (DTRs).,LABORATORY DATA:  ,White count 25,500 (26 neutrophils, 1 band, 7 lymphocytes, 1 monocyte, 1 myelocyte, 64 blasts), hemoglobin 13.3, hematocrit 38.8, and 312,000 platelets.  Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, phosphorus, uric acid, AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, and magnesium were all normal.  LDH was elevated to 1925 units/L (upper normal 670), and total protein and albumin were both low at 6.2 and 3.4 g/dL respectively.  Calcium was also slightly low at 8.8 mg/dL.  Low molecular weight heparin test was low at 0.27 units/mL.  PT was 11.8, INR 1.2, and fibrinogen 374.  Urinalysis was normal.,

llm_plan:
ASSESSMENT:

1.  **Newly Diagnosed High-Risk Precursor-B Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL):** This diagnosis is supported by the peripheral blood flow cytometry showing lymphoblasts, the elevated white blood cell count with a significant percentage of blasts (64%), and the clinical presentation of fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, and bone marrow hypermetabolism on PET/CT. The patient's age and presentation suggest a de novo diagnosis. The classification as "high-risk" is based on the information provided, though specific prognostic factors (e.g., cytogenetics, immunophenotype details beyond precursor-B) would further refine this.

2.  **Extensive Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) involving the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) and Right Iliac Vein:** This is a significant complication of the underlying malignancy, likely due to hypercoagulability associated with ALL. The patient has undergone successful interventional treatment with balloon angioplasty, mechanical and pharmacologic thrombolysis, and placement of an IVC filter. He is currently on Lovenox and was previously on Coumadin. The absence of DVT on repeat ultrasound is reassuring but requires ongoing anticoagulation.

3.  **Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS) Risk:** Given the high blast count and elevated LDH, the patient is at significant risk for TLS upon initiation of chemotherapy. Close monitoring of electrolytes and renal function will be crucial.

4.  **Potential for Bleeding:** While the patient has a history of DVT, the presence of leukemia and the initiation of chemotherapy place him at risk for bleeding complications. Careful monitoring of platelet counts and coagulation parameters is essential.

5.  **Nutritional Deficiencies:** Low total protein and albumin suggest potential malnutrition, which is common in patients with malignancy and can be exacerbated by chemotherapy.

PLAN:

1.  **Initiate Induction Chemotherapy for ALL:**
    *   **Consult Hematology/Oncology:** Urgent consultation for management of ALL and initiation of induction chemotherapy.
    *   **Chemotherapy Regimen:** Specific regimen to be determined by the Hematology/Oncology team, but will likely involve a multi-agent induction protocol (e.g., vincristine, prednisone, daunorubicin, L-asparaginase, and potentially cyclophosphamide or cytarabine, depending on risk stratification and specific ALL subtype).
    *   **Central Venous Access:** Placement of a central venous catheter (e.g., Port-a-Cath or PICC line) for administration of chemotherapy and fluids.

2.  **Management of Thrombosis:**
    *   **Anticoagulation:** Continue Lovenox 60 mg subcutaneously every 12 hours. Transition to oral anticoagulation (e.g., warfarin) once chemotherapy is initiated and stable, or maintain Lovenox based on Hematology/Oncology recommendation. Monitor INR if on warfarin.
    *   **IVC Filter Management:** Continue monitoring for signs of filter-related complications. Discuss potential removal of the IVC filter with Interventional Radiology and Hematology/Oncology once the patient is anticoagulated and the risk of recurrent DVT is deemed lower.
    *   **Monitoring for Recurrent DVT/PE:** Educate patient on signs and symptoms of DVT (leg swelling, pain, redness) and pulmonary embolism (shortness of breath, chest pain).

3.  **Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS) Prophylaxis and Monitoring:**
    *   **Hydration:** Aggressive intravenous hydration with normal saline.
    *   **Uric Acid Lowering:** Administer Allopurinol 300 mg PO daily. Consider Rasburicase if uric acid levels rise significantly despite Allopurinol.
    *   **Electrolyte Monitoring:** Frequent monitoring of electrolytes (potassium, phosphorus, calcium, uric acid) and renal function (BUN, creatinine) every 6-12 hours during induction chemotherapy. Correct any abnormalities promptly.

4.  **Supportive Care:**
    *   **Nausea/Vomiting:** Continue PRN Vicodin for pain. Consider antiemetics (e.g., ondansetron) as needed, especially with chemotherapy initiation.
    *   **Bowel Function:** Monitor for constipation and manage with stool softeners (e.g., docusate sodium) and laxatives as needed.
    *   **Nutritional Support:** Consult with a dietitian for nutritional assessment and recommendations. Consider nutritional supplements if oral intake is insufficient.
    *   **Infection Prophylaxis:** Initiate prophylactic antibiotics and antifungals as per institutional protocol for neutropenic patients.
    *   **Transfusion Support:** Monitor complete blood count (CBC) daily and transfuse packed red blood cells for symptomatic anemia or hemoglobin < 7 g/dL, and platelets for platelet count < 10,000-20,000/µL or if bleeding.

5.  **Laboratory Monitoring:**
    *   CBC with differential and peripheral blast count daily.
    *   Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) daily, including electrolytes, renal function, liver function tests, calcium, phosphorus, and uric acid.
    *   Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) daily.
    *   Coagulation studies (PT, PTT, INR, fibrinogen) daily.
    *   Low molecular weight heparin level daily while on Lovenox.

6.  **Imaging:**
    *   Consider repeat venous ultrasound of lower extremities and IVC to assess for residual thrombus or filter patency as clinically indicated.

7.  **Patient Education:**
    *   Educate patient and family regarding the diagnosis of ALL, the treatment plan, potential side effects of chemotherapy, and the importance of reporting any new symptoms promptly.
    *   Discuss the risks and benefits of all proposed treatments.

8.  **Follow-up:**
    *   Close inpatient monitoring during induction chemotherapy.
    *   Regular follow-up appointments with Hematology/Oncology after discharge.
    *   The exact timing and frequency of follow-up will be determined by the Hematology/Oncology team.

ASSESSMENT:

85-year-old female with a history of hypertension, diverticulosis, blindness, and sciatica presenting with acute onset of diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. The patient is a poor historian due to significant hearing impairment and cognitive limitations, making detailed symptom characterization difficult.

Key findings include:
*   **Dehydration:** Dry oropharynx, elevated BUN (54) and creatinine (2.2) suggesting acute kidney injury likely secondary to dehydration. Potassium is also low at 3.3.
*   **Gastroenteritis:** The constellation of diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain is highly suggestive of infectious gastroenteritis, although a specific pathogen cannot be identified without stool studies.
*   **Electrolyte Imbalance:** Hypokalemia (3.3) is present, likely exacerbated by vomiting and diarrhea.
*   **Prolonged QT Interval:** EKG demonstrates a prolonged QT interval (rate corrected QT not provided, but baseline rate is 96). This is a critical finding given the patient's age, potential electrolyte abnormalities, and medication list (Lorazepam can prolong QT).
*   **Hypertension:** Blood pressure is currently controlled, but her history of hypertension is noted.
*   **Diverticulosis:** While a potential source of abdominal pain, the acute presentation with vomiting and diarrhea makes gastroenteritis a more likely primary diagnosis.

PLAN:

1.  **Laboratory Tests:**
    *   Repeat electrolytes (sodium, potassium, bicarbonate) within 24 hours to monitor response to IV fluids and supplementation.
    *   Repeat BUN and Creatinine within 24-48 hours to assess for resolution of acute kidney injury.
    *   Stool studies: Obtain stool for culture, ova and parasites, C. difficile toxin assay, and viral panel (e.g., Norovirus, Rotavirus) to identify potential infectious etiology.
    *   Consider a lactate level if clinical suspicion for bowel ischemia arises.

2.  **Imaging Studies:**
    *   Abdominal X-ray (plain films) to rule out obstruction or perforation, given diffuse abdominal pain and vomiting, though guarding and rebound are absent.

3.  **Medications:**
    *   **IV Fluids:** Initiate intravenous fluid resuscitation with Normal Saline at 100 mL/hr, titrating based on clinical response, urine output, and laboratory values.
    *   **Potassium Supplementation:** Administer oral or IV potassium chloride as per electrolyte levels and EKG findings, with careful monitoring to avoid hyperkalemia. Target potassium > 4.0 mEq/L.
    *   **Antiemetics:** Ondansetron 4 mg IV every 8 hours as needed for nausea and vomiting.
    *   **Antidiarrheals:** Avoid antidiarrheals (e.g., loperamide) until infectious etiology is ruled out, especially if fever or bloody stools develop.
    *   **Pain Management:** Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours as needed for abdominal pain. Avoid NSAIDs due to potential for renal compromise.
    *   **Review Home Medications:** Assess the need for Lorazepam and its dosing interval. Consider discontinuing or reducing if possible, given potential for QT prolongation and central nervous system effects. Continue Klor-Con, Lexapro, and Calcium with Vitamin D as tolerated.

4.  **Referrals/Consultations:**
    *   Consider Geriatrics consultation for comprehensive management of complex medical issues in an elderly, frail patient with functional limitations.

5.  **Procedures:**
    *   None at this time.

6.  **Follow-up Plan:**
    *   Close monitoring of vital signs, fluid balance, and mental status.
    *   Re-evaluate abdominal pain and tenderness.
    *   Monitor for any signs of worsening dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, or complications of gastroenteritis (e.g., toxic megacolon, bowel perforation).
    *   If stool studies are positive for a treatable pathogen, initiate appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
    *   If abdominal X-ray is concerning for obstruction or perforation, surgical consultation will be required.
    *   Discharge planning will depend on clinical improvement, ability to tolerate oral intake, and resolution of acute kidney injury. Ensure adequate home support and follow-up instructions are provided.
    *   Follow-up with primary care physician within 1-2 weeks of discharge.

llm_plan:
ASSESSMENT:

This is an elderly female with a significant medical history including moderate to severe aortic stenosis, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and diabetes, who presented with acute onset of right-sided hemiparesis and expressive aphasia. The sudden onset and focal neurological deficits are highly concerning for an acute ischemic stroke. The presence of aphasia and right arm/hand weakness, along with mild right facial droop, strongly supports a left hemisphere vascular event.

While the patient's presentation is classic for stroke, other potential etiologies must be considered and ruled out. Her elevated white blood cell count (10,800) and significant findings on urinalysis (608 WBCs, 625 RBCs) are concerning for a urinary tract infection (UTI), which can sometimes present with altered mental status or focal neurological deficits, particularly in the elderly. However, the acute and focal nature of her neurological symptoms makes stroke the primary concern. Her elevated glucose (220) is also noted, likely related to her diabetes and stress response. The EKG findings of diffuse ST depression and biphasic T-waves are concerning and could represent demand ischemia, potentially exacerbated by the acute neurological event or underlying aortic stenosis. The elevated BUN (52) and creatinine (1.3) are consistent with her known chronic kidney disease, but warrant monitoring.

PLAN:

1.  **Neurological Workup:**
    *   **STAT Head CT with contrast:** To rule out intracranial hemorrhage and assess for early signs of ischemic stroke.
    *   **STAT CT Angiography of the Head and Neck:** To evaluate for large vessel occlusion or dissection as a potential cause of ischemic stroke.
    *   **MRI Brain with Diffusion Weighted Imaging (DWI):** If CT is negative for hemorrhage and suspicion for ischemic stroke remains high, this will be crucial for definitive diagnosis and characterization of infarct.

2.  **Cardiovascular Workup:**
    *   **STAT Cardiology Consult:** Given the significant aortic stenosis and concerning EKG findings, a cardiology consult is essential to assess for cardiac causes of stroke (e.g., valvular thrombus, atrial fibrillation) and manage potential demand ischemia.
    *   **Echocardiogram (Transthoracic):** To further evaluate the severity of aortic stenosis, assess for valvular vegetations or thrombus, and evaluate overall cardiac function.

3.  **Infectious Workup:**
    *   **Urine Culture and Sensitivity:** To guide antibiotic therapy for suspected UTI.
    *   **Blood Cultures x 2:** To rule out bacteremia, especially given the elevated WBC count.
    *   **Chest X-ray:** To rule out pneumonia as a source of infection or contributing factor to her presentation.

4.  **Laboratory Tests:**
    *   **Repeat CBC with differential:** To monitor WBC count.
    *   **Repeat BMP:** To assess electrolytes, renal function, and glucose.
    *   **Troponin:** To rule out acute myocardial infarction.
    *   **PT/INR, PTT:** To assess coagulation status, especially if thrombolysis or anticoagulation is considered.

5.  **Medications:**
    *   **Initiate Aspirin 325 mg PO:** If CT head is negative for hemorrhage and no contraindications are present, to provide antiplatelet therapy for presumed ischemic stroke.
    *   **Continue home medications:** As tolerated and appropriate, with adjustments based on ongoing assessments and specialist recommendations.
    *   **Consider IV fluids:** For hydration, especially given elevated BUN/creatinine, but monitor for fluid overload given cardiac history.
    *   **Antibiotics:** Pending urine culture results, consider empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for UTI (e.g., Ceftriaxone) if clinical suspicion is high and patient is hemodynamically stable.

6.  **Consultations:**
    *   **Neurology Consult:** For evaluation and management of suspected stroke.
    *   **Cardiology Consult:** As mentioned above.

7.  **Procedures:**
    *   **Thrombolysis (tPA):** If patient meets eligibility criteria (within time window, no contraindications on imaging) and CT is negative for hemorrhage, discuss risks and benefits of IV tPA with patient and family.
    *   **Mechanical Thrombectomy:** If large vessel occlusion is identified on CTA and patient is within the appropriate time window, discuss with interventional neurology.

8.  **Follow-up Plan:**
    *   **Continuous Neurological Monitoring:** In a stroke-capable unit.
    *   **Close monitoring of vital signs and fluid balance.**
    *   **Regular reassessment of neurological status.**
    *   **Discharge planning:** Will involve rehabilitation services (physical, occupational, speech therapy) and coordination of care with Life Care Center.
    *   **Outpatient follow-up with Neurology and Cardiology:** As indicated by inpatient course and findings.

ASSESSMENT:

1.  **Peripheral Neuropathy, likely Diabetic or related to Hydroxyurea:** The patient presents with a year-long history of progressive numbness, tingling, and sharp pain in the toes of her right foot, with some similar symptoms in the left. The symptoms are worse at night and have some radiation up the leg. While she has a history of hypertension and hypothyroidism, neither are typically primary causes of this type of neuropathy. Her thrombocythemia is being treated with hydroxyurea, which is a known potential cause of peripheral neuropathy. Given the distribution and character of her symptoms, this is a significant concern.
2.  **Essential Thrombocythemia:** The patient has a history of essential thrombocythemia, currently managed with hydroxyurea. This is a chronic condition requiring ongoing monitoring.
3.  **Hypertension:** The patient has a history of hypertension, with a current blood pressure of 140/70. This is borderline elevated and requires continued management.
4.  **Hypothyroidism:** The patient has hypothyroidism, managed with Synthroid. This is a chronic condition requiring ongoing monitoring.
5.  **Insomnia:** The patient reports insomnia, managed with Ambien and amitriptyline.
6.  **Bilateral Shoulder Pain:** The patient continues to experience bilateral shoulder pain, with a significant surgical history in both shoulders. The etiology of the current pain is unclear and may be related to chronic degenerative changes or post-surgical sequelae.
7.  **Actinic Keratosis:** A skin lesion on the right cheek was noted, described as an actinic keratosis. This requires evaluation and management.
8.  **History of Multiple Surgeries and Chronic Conditions:** The patient has an extensive surgical history and multiple chronic medical conditions, which require ongoing management and consideration in the overall care plan.

PLAN:

1.  **Peripheral Neuropathy Workup:**
    *   **Laboratory Tests:**
        *   Hemoglobin A1c: To assess for underlying diabetes or pre-diabetes as a potential cause of neuropathy.
        *   Vitamin B12 and Folate levels: To rule out nutritional deficiencies contributing to neuropathy.
        *   Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH): To ensure her hypothyroidism is adequately controlled.
        *   Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP): To assess renal and hepatic function, and electrolyte balance.
        *   Consider nerve conduction studies (NCS) and electromyography (EMG) if initial workup is unrevealing or symptoms worsen, to further characterize the neuropathy and rule out other causes like nerve compression.
    *   **Medications:**
        *   Continue current medications as prescribed.
        *   Discuss potential contribution of hydroxyurea to neuropathy with the patient. If neuropathy is deemed to be significantly related to hydroxyurea, a discussion about alternative treatments for thrombocythemia may be warranted in consultation with hematology.
        *   Consider adjusting amitriptyline dosage or adding gabapentin or pregabalin for neuropathic pain if symptoms are significantly impacting quality of life and not adequately controlled by current regimen.
    *   **Referrals/Consultations:**
        *   Referral to Neurology for formal evaluation and management of peripheral neuropathy.
    *   **Follow-up:**
        *   Follow up with Neurology as scheduled.
        *   Follow up with primary care in 4-6 weeks to review lab results and assess response to any medication adjustments.

2.  **Essential Thrombocythemia Management:**
    *   **Laboratory Tests:** Continue routine monitoring of complete blood count (CBC) with differential as per hematology recommendations.
    *   **Referrals/Consultations:** Continue follow-up with Hematology.
    *   **Follow-up:** As directed by Hematology.

3.  **Hypertension Management:**

    *   **Follow-up:** Monitor blood pressure at home and at subsequent appointments.

4.  **Hypothyroidism Management:**

    *   **Medications:** Continue Synthroid 0.1 mg daily.
    *   **Follow-up:** Review TSH results and adjust Synthroid as needed.

5.  **Insomnia Management:**
    *   **Medications:** Continue amitriptyline 50 mg at h.s. and Ambien 5 mg at h.s.
    *   **Follow-up:** Assess effectiveness of current regimen at next visit. Discuss sleep hygiene.

ASSESSMENT:

The patient presents with a constellation of symptoms including backache, stomachache, dysuria, fever, and cough, which began acutely over the last two days. Her urinalysis is highly suggestive of a urinary tract infection (UTI), with positive findings for leukocyte esterase, nitrites, significant white blood cells, and bacteria. The presence of blood and protein in the urine, along with flank tenderness, raises concern for pyelonephritis (kidney infection), especially given her history of kidney stones and prior UTI less than a year ago. The fever and cough, while potentially unrelated, could also indicate a concurrent respiratory infection or a more systemic inflammatory process. Her cardiac history and associated activity limitations are noted but do not appear to be the primary driver of her current acute symptoms.

PLAN:

1.  **Laboratory Tests:**
    *   Urine culture and sensitivity results are pending and will be crucial for guiding antibiotic therapy.
    *   Complete blood count (CBC) with differential to assess for leukocytosis and signs of systemic infection.
    *   Basic metabolic panel (BMP) to assess renal function and electrolytes, given her history of kidney stones and potential for pyelonephritis.

2.  **Imaging Studies:**
    *   Consider a renal ultrasound to evaluate for any obstructing stones or hydronephrosis, given her history of kidney stones and current flank tenderness. This can be deferred pending urine culture results and clinical response to initial treatment.

3.  **Medications:**
    *   Prescribe **Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg (Bactrim DS) two tablets by mouth twice daily for 7 days**. This is a common first-line treatment for uncomplicated UTIs and pyelonephritis. Given her flank tenderness and fever, a 7-day course is appropriate.
    *   Recommend **Acetaminophen 650 mg by mouth every 6 hours as needed for fever and pain**.
    *   Advise **Ibuprofen 400 mg by mouth every 6-8 hours as needed for pain and inflammation**, provided no contraindications.

4.  **Referrals or Consultations:**
    *   No immediate referrals are necessary at this time.

5.  **Procedures:**
    *   No procedures are indicated at this time.

6.  **Follow-up Plan:**
    *   **Return to clinic in 3-5 days for re-evaluation** to assess symptom improvement and review urine culture results.
    *   **Educate patient on signs and symptoms of worsening infection**, including increased fever, severe flank pain, nausea, vomiting, or inability to tolerate oral intake, and advise to seek immediate medical attention if these occur.
    *   **Advise increased fluid intake** (water) to help flush the urinary tract.
    *   **Reinforce avoidance of decongestants** as per her history.
    *   **Follow up on pending urine culture results** and adjust antibiotic therapy if necessary based on sensitivity patterns.
    *   **Schedule a follow-up appointment in 2-3 weeks** to ensure complete resolution of symptoms and discuss any further management if indicated by imaging or persistent symptoms.

llm_plan:
ASSESSMENT:
69-year-old male with a history of atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presenting with acute onset altered mental status. The patient's speech is coherent but nonsensical. Initial workup including head CT from an outlying facility was negative for acute intracranial pathology. EKG shows atrial fibrillation without acute ischemia. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly, but no acute pulmonary process. Laboratory data is largely unremarkable, with the exception of a slightly elevated glucose (161) and creatinine (1.4). Troponin is mildly elevated at 0.09, which warrants further investigation.

Given the patient's history of atrial fibrillation, the possibility of a cardioembolic stroke causing the altered mental status must be considered, despite the negative head CT. The nonsensical speech could represent aphasia or other cognitive impairment secondary to a cerebrovascular event. The mild troponin elevation could be related to underlying cardiac strain from the atrial fibrillation or a new cardiac event, though less likely given the negative serial isoenzymes (assuming the single value provided is the initial one). Other differentials for altered mental status include metabolic derangements (though labs are largely normal), infection (no fever, normal WBC), or a primary neurological event not visualized on CT (e.g., posterior circulation stroke, lacunar infarct). The patient's current medications include Plavix and aspirin, which is dual antiplatelet therapy, and Lotensin and Toprol for hypertension.

PLAN:
1.  **Laboratory Tests:**
    *   Repeat troponin and serial cardiac enzymes to assess for evolving myocardial injury.
    *   Basic metabolic panel to re-evaluate electrolytes and renal function.
    *   Complete blood count to monitor for any changes.
    *   Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) to rule out thyroid dysfunction as a cause of altered mental status.
    *   Urine drug screen to rule out substance-induced delirium.
    *   Consider ammonia level if hepatic encephalopathy is suspected, though no overt signs of liver disease are present.

2.  **Imaging Studies:**
    *   MRI Brain with and without contrast to better evaluate for ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, particularly in the posterior circulation or smaller lacunar infarcts not seen on CT.
    *   Echocardiogram (transthoracic) to assess for valvular abnormalities, mural thrombus, or other structural heart disease that could predispose to cardioembolism.

3.  **Medications:**
    *   Continue current medications: Lotensin 20 mg daily, Toprol 50 mg daily, Plavix 75 mg daily, and aspirin 81 mg daily. Given the history of atrial fibrillation and suspected stroke, continuation of dual antiplatelet therapy is appropriate pending further evaluation.
    *   Consider starting a statin if not already on one, or optimizing current statin therapy, given history of hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular risk factors. (Note: Hyperlipidemia is listed in PMH, but no statin is listed in current meds. This needs clarification and likely initiation/adjustment).

4.  **Referrals or Consultations:**
    *   Neurology consultation for evaluation and management of suspected stroke and altered mental status.
    *   Cardiology consultation to evaluate atrial fibrillation management and assess for underlying cardiac causes of potential embolic events.

5.  **Procedures:**
    *   None at this time.

6.  **Follow-up Plan:**
    *   Close monitoring of vital signs and neurological status.
    *   Follow up on all pending laboratory and imaging results.
    *   Admit to the hospital for further workup and management.
    *   Discharge planning will be dependent on the results of the workup and patient's clinical improvement. If a stroke is confirmed, speech and occupational therapy will be initiated.

llm_plan:
ASSESSMENT:
54-year-old male, occupational blood-borne pathogen exposure (Hepatitis C positive source, HIV negative source), presenting for final evaluation after a needle stick injury to the left index finger. The patient reports adherence to post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) if initiated, though this is not explicitly stated in the note, it is standard practice. He denies symptoms of acute viral illness prior to yesterday, but now reports nausea, vomiting, and decreased appetite. Physical exam is unremarkable, with no signs of acute viral hepatitis or local infection at the injury site. Given the known Hepatitis C positive source and the patient's recent onset of gastrointestinal symptoms, there is a concern for acute Hepatitis C infection. However, these symptoms are non-specific and could also be attributed to other causes. The HIV negative status of the source patient significantly reduces the risk of HIV transmission.

PLAN:
1.  **Laboratory Tests:**
    *   Hepatitis C RNA, quantitative (HCV RNA, viral load) - to assess for acute infection.
    *   Hepatitis C antibody - to confirm seroconversion if RNA is positive.
    *   Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), Hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs), Hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) - to ensure Hepatitis B vaccination status and rule out co-infection.
    *   HIV antibody/antigen test - baseline and follow-up as per PEP guidelines, though source was negative.
    *   Liver Function Tests (LFTs): ALT, AST, Bilirubin (total and direct), Alkaline Phosphatase, Albumin, PT/INR - to assess for baseline liver function and any signs of hepatic inflammation.

2.  **Medications:**
    *   Continue any prescribed post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for Hepatitis C if initiated by employee health or ED. (Note: PEP for Hep C is not standard of care and is generally not recommended unless specific high-risk factors are present and discussed with infectious disease specialist. The plan assumes this was considered and potentially initiated or ruled out by previous evaluations).
    *   Symptomatic management for nausea/vomiting: Ondansetron 4mg PO every 8 hours as needed.
    *   Advise patient to maintain hydration and a bland diet.

3.  **Referrals/Consultations:**
    *   Consider consultation with Infectious Disease specialist if Hepatitis C RNA is positive to guide management and treatment.
    *   Continue follow-up with Employee Health for ongoing monitoring and management.

4.  **Procedures:**
    *   None at this time.

5.  **Follow-up Plan:**
    *   Return to clinic in 2-4 weeks for review of laboratory results and clinical assessment.
    *   If HCV RNA is positive, close monitoring and treatment will be initiated.
    *   If HCV RNA is negative and antibodies remain negative at 6 months post-exposure, the risk of transmission is considered very low.
    *   Educate patient on signs and symptoms of Hepatitis C (jaundice, fatigue, abdominal pain, nausea) and to report any new or worsening symptoms immediately.
    *   Reinforce universal precautions for future exposures.

**ASSESSMENT:**

1.  **Allergic Rhinitis:** The patient presents with classic symptoms of nasal congestion, stuffiness, and clear nasal discharge. Her mother is also experiencing allergy symptoms, suggesting a potential environmental trigger. The pale nasal mucosa with clear discharge on examination is highly suggestive of allergic rhinitis. Her current use of Zyrtec indicates a history of allergic symptoms, and it is possible her current dose or frequency is insufficient, or she is experiencing a flare-up.

2.  **Developmental Milestones:**
    *   **Language:** Speaking in sentences is appropriate for a 2-year-old.
    *   **Cognitive:** Not knowing colors is within the normal range for a 2-year-old, though some may be starting to recognize basic colors. Knowing some shapes is also appropriate.
    *   **Toilet Training:** Lack of interest in potty training is very common at this age. Most children are not ready for formal toilet training until closer to 2.5-3 years old.
    *   **Growth:** Height and weight in the 80th percentile are appropriate. Head circumference over the 95th percentile, while noted, is stable and has been a consistent finding, and in the absence of other neurological concerns or rapid changes, is likely constitutional.

**PLAN:**

1.  **Allergic Rhinitis Management:**
    *   **Medication:** Continue Zyrtec (cetirizine) 5mg once daily. Advise mom to try giving it consistently every day for the next 2-4 weeks to see if it provides adequate symptom control. If symptoms persist despite daily Zyrtec, consider increasing the dose to 10mg once daily, or switching to a different antihistamine such as loratadine or fexofenadine.
    *   **Nasal Saline:** Recommend daily nasal saline rinses or sprays to help clear nasal passages and reduce congestion.
    *   **Environmental Control:** Discuss strategies to minimize allergen exposure, such as keeping windows closed during high pollen seasons, using air purifiers, and regular vacuuming.
    *   **Education:** Educate mom on the chronic nature of allergic rhinitis and the importance of consistent medication use.

2.  **Developmental Monitoring:**
    *   **Toilet Training:** Reassure mom that her daughter's lack of interest in potty training is normal for her age. Advise her to continue offering opportunities for potty use without pressure and to wait for signs of readiness (e.g., staying dry for longer periods, showing interest in the toilet, communicating the need to go).
    *   **Cognitive/Language:** Continue to encourage age-appropriate activities that promote color and shape recognition, reading books, and conversation.

3.  **Allergies:** Continue to strictly avoid eggs and peanuts. Ensure epinephrine auto-injector is available if prescribed for any other severe allergies.

4.  **Follow-up:**
    *   Return to clinic in 4-6 weeks for a well-child check, or sooner if symptoms worsen, or if there are concerns about medication side effects or continued poor symptom control of allergic rhinitis.
    *   At the next visit, we will reassess her allergic rhinitis symptoms and discuss further management if needed. We will also continue to monitor her developmental progress.

ASSESSMENT:

12-year-old male with a 10-day history of clear nasal discharge, sinus congestion, and mild headache, with a history of significant allergies, particularly to ragweed. Physical exam reveals pale nasal mucosa with clear discharge, otherwise unremarkable. He is currently on Advair and Allegra, with subjective worsening of allergy symptoms despite Allegra.

Given the clear nasal discharge, absence of fever, and history of allergies, the most likely diagnosis is allergic rhinitis, possibly with a superimposed viral upper respiratory infection, or a significant exacerbation of his underlying allergic rhinitis. The pale nasal mucosa is classic for allergic rhinitis. The lack of purulent discharge or fever makes bacterial sinusitis less likely at this time.

PLAN:

1.  **Medications:**
    *   Continue Advair as prescribed.

ASSESSMENT:
5-year-old male with a history of recent left otitis media treated with amoxicillin, now presenting with recurrent left ear pain and persistent thick, purulent nasal discharge. The physical exam reveals bilateral tympanic membranes (TMs) that are gray in color with distorted light reflexes, suggestive of middle ear effusion. There is significant postnasal discharge and swollen, red nares with purulent drainage, consistent with acute rhinosinusitis. The lack of fever and clear lung sounds make pneumonia less likely, and the absence of wheezing or shortness of breath makes asthma exacerbation or bronchitis unlikely at this time. Given the persistent symptoms and recent antibiotic treatment, this is likely a case of recurrent acute otitis media (left ear) and acute bacterial rhinosinusitis. The family history of recurrent ear infections and URIs in siblings also suggests a potential predisposition.

ASSESSMENT:
1.  **Chronic Nasal Congestion:** This 11-year-old female presents with persistent nasal congestion and snorting, despite discontinuation of Allegra following an allergist evaluation that revealed no allergies. Physical exam shows some swelling of the left turbinates. This suggests a non-allergic rhinitis etiology, potentially related to environmental irritants, viral post-nasal drip, or possibly adenoid hypertrophy given her age and symptoms.
2.  **Right Great Toe Erythema and Peeling:** The patient has a one-and-a-half-week history of redness, erythema, and mild skin peeling on the lateral aspect of her right great toe. The skin is dry, and there is no bleeding or oozing. Her toenails are noted to be very short on both feet, including the affected toe. This presentation is concerning for a fungal infection (tinea pedis) or possibly a contact dermatitis. The short toenails could be a predisposing factor for fungal infections or a result of self-treatment.

PLAN:
1.  **Nasal Congestion:**
    *   **Medications:** Recommend a trial of intranasal corticosteroid spray (e.g., fluticasone propionate 50 mcg spray, 1 spray in each nostril once daily) for 4 weeks to reduce turbinate inflammation. Advise saline nasal rinses twice daily to help clear mucus.
    *   **Referral/Consultation:** If symptoms do not improve significantly after 4 weeks of intranasal steroids and saline rinses, consider referral to ENT for evaluation of possible adenoid hypertrophy or other structural causes of chronic congestion.
    *   **Follow-up:** Re-evaluate in 4 weeks to assess response to treatment.

2.  **Right Great Toe Erythema and Peeling:**
    *   **Laboratory Tests:** Consider a KOH preparation of skin scrapings from the affected area to rule out fungal infection.
    *   **Medications:** If KOH is positive for fungus, prescribe a topical antifungal cream (e.g., clotrimazole 1% cream, apply to affected area twice daily for 2-4 weeks). If KOH is negative or if symptoms are mild and clinical suspicion for fungal infection remains high, a trial of topical antifungal may still be initiated. If contact dermatitis is suspected and fungal infection is ruled out, a mild topical corticosteroid (e.g., hydrocortisone 1% cream) could be considered for short-term use.
    *   **Patient Education:** Advise patient to keep the area clean and dry, wear breathable footwear, and avoid sharing socks or shoes. Discuss proper toenail care, recommending to keep them trimmed but not excessively short.
    *   **Follow-up:** Re-evaluate in 2-3 weeks to assess response to treatment. If symptoms worsen or do not improve, further investigation or referral to dermatology may be warranted.

ASSESSMENT:

49-year-old female with a history of atopic dermatitis presenting with a three-week history of left otalgia, headache, left-sided sinus pressure, and left jaw pain. She reports improvement in hearing difficulty. She denies fever, cough, or sore throat. Physical exam reveals left tympanic membrane effusion, otherwise unremarkable findings in the ears, nose, throat, neck, and lungs. Her vital signs are stable.

The constellation of symptoms, including otalgia, sinus pressure, and jaw pain, in the setting of a recent improvement in hearing, is concerning for a subacute or chronic inflammatory process affecting the middle ear and/or sinuses. Given her history of sinusitis and atopic dermatitis, which can predispose to inflammatory conditions, a diagnosis of left otitis media with effusion and possible chronic rhinosinusitis is considered. The jaw pain could be referred from the otitis or related to temporomandibular joint dysfunction, though the latter is less likely given the other symptoms. The chronic left-sided headache is also a significant component, which may be exacerbated by the current inflammatory process.

PLAN:

1.  **Laboratory Tests:**

2.  **Imaging Studies:**

3.  **Medications:**

llm_plan:
ASSESSMENT:

75-year-old female with a history of heart disease, hypertension, type II diabetes, and pulmonary embolism presenting with worsening weakness, shakiness, and dyspnea on exertion. The patient is a poor historian and is not currently on any regular medications for her chronic conditions.

Differential diagnoses include:
1.  **Exacerbation of underlying heart disease:** Given her history of heart disease, hypertension, and family history of cardiovascular disease, worsening heart failure or ischemic heart disease is a strong possibility. The dyspnea on exertion is concerning.
2.  **Pulmonary embolism:** Despite a history of PE, her current symptoms of dyspnea on exertion could represent a new or recurrent PE, although the absence of pleuritic chest pain or hemoptysis makes this less likely.
3.  **Anemia:** Weakness and fatigue can be symptoms of anemia, which can be exacerbated by underlying chronic conditions.
4.  **Deconditioning:** While her symptoms are worsening, a degree of deconditioning could contribute to her exertional dyspnea and weakness.
5.  **Medication non-adherence/discontinuation:** The patient is not aware of her current medications, raising concerns about whether she is taking them as prescribed, or if they have been discontinued. This could lead to decompensation of her underlying chronic conditions.
6.  **Electrolyte imbalance/Hypoglycemia:** Given her history of diabetes and potential for medication non-adherence, these are possibilities contributing to her weakness and shakiness.

PLAN:

1.  **Laboratory Tests:**
    *   Complete Blood Count (CBC) with differential: To assess for anemia.
    *   Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP): To evaluate electrolytes, renal function, and glucose.
    *   B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP): To assess for heart failure.
    *   Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH): To rule out thyroid dysfunction contributing to fatigue.
    *   Hemoglobin A1c: To assess glycemic control given history of Type II Diabetes.
    *   Troponin I: To rule out acute myocardial infarction, given nonspecific ST changes on EKG.

2.  **Imaging Studies:**
    *   Chest X-ray: To evaluate for pulmonary congestion, infiltrates, or other cardiopulmonary pathology. (Pending)
    *   Echocardiogram: To assess cardiac structure and function, particularly ventricular function and valvular integrity.
    *   Consider CT Pulmonary Angiogram (CTPA) if suspicion for PE remains high after initial workup, especially if BNP is elevated or other risk factors are identified.

3.  **Medications:**
    *   Initiate Lisinopril 10 mg PO daily for hypertension and heart failure management.
    *   Initiate Metformin 500 mg PO BID for Type II Diabetes.
    *   Initiate Atorvastatin 20 mg PO daily for hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular risk reduction.
    *   Provide patient with written prescriptions and clear instructions for all new medications. Educate on the importance of adherence.

4.  **Referrals/Consultations:**
    *   Cardiology consultation: To further evaluate her underlying heart disease, optimize management, and assess for need for further cardiac workup.
    *   Consider Geriatrics consultation: To assist with medication reconciliation, management of multiple chronic conditions, and assessment of functional status.

5.  **Procedures:**
    *   None at this time.

6.  **Follow-up Plan:**
    *   Return to clinic in 1-2 weeks for review of laboratory results, medication tolerance, and symptom assessment.
    *   Follow up with Cardiology as scheduled.
    *   Encourage patient to call immediately if symptoms worsen significantly, or if she develops chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or syncope.
    *   Assist patient in obtaining a pill organizer and ensure she has a reliable method for medication adherence. Explore potential for home health services if needed for medication management and monitoring.
llm_dx_summary: A 75-year-old female with multiple chronic conditions presents with worsening weakness, shakiness, and dyspnea on exertion, most likely due to exacerbation of underlying heart disease with consideration of other contributing factors including pulmonary embolism, anemia, and medication non-adherence.

llm_plan:
ASSESSMENT:

77-year-old female presenting with diffuse joint pain, particularly in the hands and wrists, which is impacting her mobility. She reports no significant swelling or erythema, but notes increased discomfort. Her current NSAID, Daypro, is not providing relief.

This presentation, coupled with the physical exam finding of "doughiness" in the MCP joints and wrists, raises concern for an inflammatory arthropathy. While she has a history of lumbar discitis and prior pulmonary embolism, her current symptoms are distinct. The absence of fever, chills, or significant swelling makes acute infectious arthritis less likely. Given her age and the distribution of pain, osteoarthritis is a consideration, but the "doughiness" suggests a component of synovitis. Rheumatoid arthritis is a strong possibility, especially given the bilateral involvement of MCP joints. Other inflammatory arthropathies like psoriatic arthritis or reactive arthritis are less likely given the lack of characteristic skin/nail changes or recent infectious symptoms, respectively.

Her other medical issues are relatively stable:
*   **Hypertension:** BP is elevated at 140/64-148/60, but she is on multiple medications.
*   **Diabetes Mellitus Type 2:** Hemoglobin A1C is well-controlled at 5.3. Her glucose is only slightly elevated at 116.
*   **Chronic Kidney Disease:** BUN of 54 and Creatinine of 1.4 suggest Stage 3 CKD, likely related to her hypertension and diabetes.
*   **Anemia:** Mild anemia (Hgb 10.5) is noted, which could be related to chronic disease, iron deficiency, or other factors.
*   **Hyperlipidemia:** Cholesterol and LDL are borderline elevated.
*   **Hypothyroidism:** TSH is normal, indicating her Synthroid dose is adequate.
*   **Osteoporosis:** She is on Miacalcin and Ogen, but her calcium is borderline elevated at 10.8.
*   **History of PE:** This is a significant past medical history and needs to be considered with any new treatment plans.
*   **Depression:** She has restarted Zoloft due to feeling depressed and lethargic, which may be contributing to her decreased mobility and perception of pain.
*   **History of C. difficile colitis:** This has resolved.

PLAN:

1.  **Musculoskeletal:**
    *   **Diagnosis:** Suspected inflammatory arthropathy, likely Rheumatoid Arthritis.
    *   **Labs:**
        *   Rheumatoid Factor (RF)
        *   Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies
        *   Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)
        *   C-Reactive Protein (CRP)
        *   Complete Blood Count (CBC) with differential (to re-evaluate anemia and look for other abnormalities)
        *   Iron studies (ferritin, iron, TIBC) to further assess anemia.
    *   **Imaging:**
        *   X-rays of bilateral hands and wrists to assess for erosions, joint space narrowing, and other signs of arthritis.
    *   **Medications:**
        *   Discontinue Daypro (Oxaprozin) as it is ineffective.
        *   Initiate Methotrexate 10 mg PO weekly. This is a first-line treatment for RA.
        *   Prescribe Folic Acid 1 mg PO daily (except on the day of methotrexate) to mitigate side effects.
        *   Consider a short course of Prednisone 10 mg daily for rapid symptom relief while waiting for methotrexate to take effect, to be tapered over 2-4 weeks.
    *   **Referral:**
        *   Rheumatology consultation for definitive diagnosis and management of suspected inflammatory arthritis.
    *   **Patient Education:** Discuss the suspected diagnosis, the rationale for starting methotrexate, potential side effects, and the importance of adherence. Educate on the need for regular monitoring of blood counts and liver function tests.

2.  **Cardiovascular:**
    *   **Hypertension:** Continue current medications (Nifedipine-XR, furosemide, lisinopril). Monitor blood pressure closely. Given her elevated readings, consider a slight increase in lisinopril to 30 mg daily if tolerated and renal function allows.
    *   **Hyperlipidemia:** Continue gemfibrozil. Recheck lipid panel in 3-6 months.

3.  **Endocrine:**
    *   **Diabetes Mellitus Type 2:** Continue current management. Her A1C is excellent. Monitor blood sugars.
    *   **Hypothyroidism:** Continue Synthroid. TSH is normal.
    *   **Osteoporosis:** Continue Miacalcin and Ogen. Monitor calcium levels. Given the borderline elevation, consider discussing alternative or adjunctive therapies with her endocrinologist or rheumatologist, especially if starting methotrexate.

4.  **Renal:**
    *   **Chronic Kidney Disease:** Monitor BUN and Creatinine with routine labs. Ensure adequate hydration. Avoid nephrotoxic agents where possible.

5.  **Hematologic:**
    *   **Anemia:** Further workup as outlined above (CBC, iron studies). Address underlying cause.

6.  **Psychiatric:**
    *   **Depression:** Continue Zoloft. Monitor for improvement in mood, energy, and sleep. Discuss the impact of her physical limitations on her mood.

7.  **General/Preventative:**
    *   **Smoking Cessation:** Strongly advise smoking cessation. Provide resources and discuss strategies. Smoking is a significant risk factor for RA and cardiovascular disease.
    *   **Follow-up:**
        *   Return to clinic in 4 weeks for assessment of response to methotrexate and prednisone (if prescribed), review of lab results, and to discuss Rheumatology recommendations.
        *   Continue routine follow-up for management of chronic conditions.
        *   Pap smear was done today.

8.  **Medication Reconciliation:** Review all current medications for potential interactions and necessity, especially with the addition of methotrexate and potential prednisone. Ensure patient understands dosing and schedule.

ASSESSMENT:

Following removal, there was noted erythema and some bloody drainage, consistent with local irritation and inflammation from the retained object. The foul odor has resolved with removal.

However, his physical examination of the abdomen and back was entirely benign, with no tenderness, distension, or organomegaly. He is otherwise acting normally, eating and drinking well, and has no fevers or changes in bowel or bladder habits reported by the parents. The abdominal pain is not significantly impacting his activity level. Given the benign abdominal exam and lack of other systemic symptoms, the abdominal pain is likely functional or related to mild constipation, as suggested by the X-ray showing stool in the vault. The urine analysis was also unremarkable.

    *   No further imaging studies are indicated at this time. The abdominal X-ray was obtained for evaluation of abdominal pain and showed stool, which is being addressed.
5.  **Procedures:**
    *   Foreign body removal from the right nasal cavity was successfully completed in the ED.
6.  **Referrals/Consultations:**
    *   No referrals or consultations are indicated at this time.
7.  **Follow-up:**
    *   Follow up with your pediatrician in 1-2 weeks for routine care and to re-evaluate the abdominal pain if it persists or worsens.

llm_plan:
ASSESSMENT:
50-year-old female presenting with several months of worsening mood swings, tearfulness, difficulty concentrating, and insomnia, impacting her work. She denies suicidal ideation, hot flashes, or night sweats. She has a history of a positive response to Wellbutrin in the past for overeating-related obsessive-compulsive symptoms, though it was not covered by insurance at that time. She has no other prior antidepressant use. She underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH-BSO) in December 2003. Given her age, surgical history of BSO, and current mood symptoms, **perimenopausal mood disorder** is a primary concern. The symptoms of mood lability, tearfulness, and insomnia are consistent with hormonal fluctuations or deficiency. The past positive response to Wellbutrin suggests a potential benefit from serotonergic or dopaminergic agents, but the current presentation warrants a broader approach considering the menopausal status.

PLAN:
1.  **Laboratory Tests:**
    *   TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone): To rule out hypothyroidism as a contributor to mood symptoms and fatigue.
    *   CBC (Complete Blood Count): To assess for anemia, which can cause fatigue and affect mood.
    *   BMP (Basic Metabolic Panel): To assess electrolyte balance and renal function.
    *   Consider FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone) and Estradiol levels if symptoms are highly suggestive of significant menopausal transition and to guide potential hormone replacement therapy.

2.  **Medications:**
    *   **Bupropion XL (Wellbutrin XL):** Prescribe 150 mg daily. Given her prior positive response and the absence of significant anxiety or panic symptoms, this is a reasonable first-line agent. It can also help with energy and concentration.
    *   Discuss potential side effects including insomnia, dry mouth, and headache. Advise to take in the morning to minimize sleep disturbance.

3.  **Referrals/Consultations:**
    *   **Gynecology:** For evaluation of menopausal symptoms and discussion of potential hormone replacement therapy (HRT) options, given her history of TAH-BSO. This will be crucial for long-term management of menopausal symptoms.

4.  **Procedures:**
    *   None at this time.

5.  **Follow-up Plan:**
    *   **Return to clinic in 4-6 weeks** to assess response to Bupropion XL, review lab results, and discuss findings from the gynecology consultation.
    *   Encourage lifestyle modifications including regular exercise, a balanced diet, and stress management techniques.
    *   Provide patient education on perimenopause and mood disorders.
    *   If no significant improvement with Bupropion XL or if HRT is initiated and symptoms persist, consider alternative or adjunctive pharmacotherapy, or referral to psychiatry.

**ASSESSMENT:**

1.  **Asthma, poorly controlled:** The patient reports worsening asthma symptoms over the past three months, requiring daily use of her rescue inhaler (Proventil). This is likely exacerbated by increased allergen exposure (corn dust from husband's work) and non-adherence to her prescribed nasal steroid (Flonase) for allergic rhinitis. Her previous positive response to Flonase suggests allergic rhinitis is a significant trigger for her asthma. The reported vaginal irritation with Advair in the past warrants consideration for alternative long-acting inhaled corticosteroids if a controller medication is deemed necessary.

2.  **Allergic Rhinitis, exacerbation:** Increased exposure to corn dust and reduced use of Flonase have likely contributed to worsening allergy symptoms.

3.  **Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) / Perimenopausal symptoms:** The patient describes cyclical mood changes (irritability, impatience) in the week preceding her menses, which improve with the onset of her period. While this pattern is classic for PMS, at age 42, perimenopausal changes should also be considered, especially given her report of menses being somewhat shorter and occasional spotting post-cycle, though she denies hot flashes or night sweats.

4.  **Vaginal Discharge:** The patient presents with a moderate amount of thick white/yellow vaginal discharge. This requires further evaluation to determine the etiology, which could range from normal physiological discharge to an infectious process.

5.  **History of UTI with positive blood, unconfirmed resolution:** The chart notes a previous UTI with 3+ blood, and the urine has not been rechecked. This needs to be addressed to ensure resolution and rule out any underlying renal or urinary tract pathology.

**PLAN:**

1.  **Asthma/Allergic Rhinitis:**
    *   **Medications:**
        *   Restart Flonase (fluticasone propionate) nasal spray 2 sprays in each nostril once daily. Counsel on consistent daily use for optimal effect.
        *   Initiate a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) controller medication. Given her history of vaginal irritation with Advair, consider a different ICS/long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) combination such as Symbicort (budesonide/formoterol) or Dulera (mometasone/formoterol) 160/4.5 mcg, 2 puffs inhaled twice daily. Discuss potential side effects and alternatives if needed.
        *   Continue Proventil (albuterol) MDI as needed for acute symptom relief.
        *   Resume Allegra (fexofenadine) 180 mg daily for allergy symptoms.
    *   **Patient Education:** Discuss triggers for asthma and allergies, particularly corn dust. Advise on environmental controls and potential need for mask use during high exposure periods. Reinforce proper inhaler technique.

2.  **Vaginal Discharge:**
    *   **Laboratory Tests:**
        *   Wet mount microscopy of vaginal discharge to assess for yeast, bacterial vaginosis, and trichomoniasis.
        *   Gram stain and culture of vaginal discharge if indicated by wet mount findings or high suspicion for bacterial infection.
        *   Consider Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT) for Chlamydia and Gonorrhea, given the discharge, although less likely given her marital status and lack of other symptoms.
    *   **Medications:** Treatment will be guided by laboratory results.

3.  **Premenstrual Syndrome / Perimenopausal Symptoms:**
    *   **Patient Education:** Discuss the cyclical nature of her mood symptoms and reassure her that this is common. Explain the potential for perimenopausal changes at her age.
    *   **Follow-up:** Monitor symptoms. If mood changes become significantly disruptive or if other perimenopausal symptoms develop (hot flashes, night sweats, significant menstrual irregularities), further evaluation and management options can be discussed.

4.  **History of UTI:**
    *   **Laboratory Tests:** Urinalysis with microscopy and urine culture and sensitivity.
    *   **Patient Education:** Emphasize the importance of completing any prescribed antibiotic course if a new infection is diagnosed.

5.  **Cholesterol Results:**
    *   **Follow-up:** Review cholesterol results once available. If abnormal, discuss management strategies including lifestyle modifications and potential pharmacotherapy.

6.  **Follow-up:**
    *   Schedule a follow-up appointment in 4-6 weeks to review lab results (vaginal discharge, urine), assess response to new asthma/allergy medications, and discuss any further concerns.
    *   Instruct the patient to call sooner if her asthma symptoms worsen significantly, she develops fever, or experiences new concerning symptoms.

ASSESSMENT:

1.  **Folliculitis with secondary infection/abscess formation:** The patient presents with multiple inflamed hair follicles and small abscesses on her inner thighs, which she has been squeezing, leading to bruising and irritation. This is consistent with a bacterial infection of the hair follicles.
2.  **Pelvic pain, likely secondary to prior gynecological issues:** The patient reports significant pelvic pain and a desire to see a previous physician for this. 3.  **Bipolar Disorder, likely poorly controlled after lithium discontinuation:** The patient reports significant mood swings, anger outbursts, and difficulty coping since discontinuing lithium. PLAN:

1.  **Folliculitis/Abscess Management:**
    *   **Medications:**
        *   Prescribe topical antibiotic ointment (e.g., mupirocin 2% ointment) to apply to affected areas twice daily.

ASSESSMENT:
This is a two-and-a-half-month-old male presenting with a three to four-day history of cough and congestion, associated with decreased appetite. The patient has no fever, rhinorrhea, or sick contacts. He has no known smoke exposure. The physical examination is largely unremarkable, with the exception of a slightly elevated respiratory rate (though noted to be much slower and regular during the physician's exam compared to nursing assessment) and a clear chest x-ray. The absence of fever, significant respiratory distress, apnea, or other concerning symptoms, coupled with a clear chest x-ray, makes a serious lower respiratory tract infection such as pneumonia less likely. The symptoms are most consistent with an upper respiratory infection (URI) or viral syndrome, which is common in this age group. The decreased appetite is likely secondary to the general malaise associated with the illness.

PLAN:
1.  **Supportive Care:** Advise parents on supportive measures for viral illness in infants, including:
    *   **Hydration:** Encourage frequent, smaller feeds to maintain adequate hydration. Monitor for signs of dehydration (e.g., decreased wet diapers, sunken fontanelle, lethargy).
    *   **Nasal Saline and Suctioning:** Recommend saline nasal drops followed by gentle bulb suctioning to clear nasal congestion, especially before feeds and sleep.
    *   **Humidification:** Suggest using a cool-mist humidifier in the infant's room to help with congestion.
    *   **Rest:** Encourage adequate rest.
2.  **Monitoring:** Instruct parents to closely monitor the infant for any signs of worsening, including:
    *   Increased work of breathing (retractions, grunting, nasal flaring)
    *   Fever (temperature > 100.4°F or 38°C)
    *   Apnea (pauses in breathing)
    *   Lethargy or decreased responsiveness
    *   Inability to feed or signs of dehydration
    *   Worsening cough
3.  **Medications:** No specific medications are indicated at this time given the likely viral etiology and absence of fever or significant distress. Avoid cough and cold medications in infants under 2 years of age.
4.  **Follow-up:**
    *   **Return Precautions:** Advise parents to return to the emergency department or seek immediate medical attention if any of the worsening signs listed above develop.
    *   **Routine Follow-up:** Schedule a follow-up appointment with the pediatrician in 5-7 days for re-evaluation, or sooner if symptoms do not begin to improve or if concerns arise.
5.  **Education:** Reassure parents that most viral illnesses in infants are self-limiting and that supportive care is the mainstay of treatment. Discuss the importance of hand hygiene to prevent spread.

llm_plan:
ASSESSMENT:

This is a 2-month-old female presenting with a 1-week history of congestion, fever, cough, and decreased oral intake. The mother reports irregular and rapid breathing with retractions, paroxysmal cough with post-tussive emesis, and short respiratory pauses following coughing spells. She also notes regurgitation after feedings and decreased wet diapers. Her temperature has ranged between 102-104°F. Her brother has similar URI symptoms.

Key findings from the physical exam include mild tachypnea (RR 30), a few faint rales in the lungs, and a temperature of 100.4°F. Vital signs are otherwise stable with HR 140 and SpO2 100%. The infant is described as well-appearing and in no acute distress.

Laboratory data shows a white blood cell count of 12.4 with a left shift (3 bands), hemoglobin of 10.1, and elevated platelets of 611,000. C-reactive protein is 0.3, which is not significantly elevated. Urinalysis shows 10-25 bacteria, which is likely a contaminant given the absence of other UTI symptoms and the patient's age. Chest x-ray shows no acute disease with the exception of a small retrocardiac density on the posterior view, which is nonspecific and could represent atelectasis or a small infiltrate.

The constellation of symptoms, particularly the paroxysmal cough, post-tussive emesis, and respiratory pauses, in a young infant raises concern for a significant lower respiratory tract infection, potentially pertussis or a viral bronchiolitis with secondary bacterial concern. The elevated WBC with a left shift and elevated platelets, while not definitive, are suggestive of an inflammatory process. The retrocardiac density on CXR is concerning for a possible pneumonia, although it is small. Given the age and symptoms, ruling out serious bacterial infection is important.

1.  **Suspected Bronchiolitis/Viral Pneumonia:** The cough, congestion, tachypnea, and rales are consistent with a viral lower respiratory tract infection. The paroxysmal nature of the cough and post-tussive emesis could also suggest pertussis, though this is less common in vaccinated infants and vaccination status is not provided.
2.  **Rule out Pneumonia:** The retrocardiac density on CXR warrants consideration of pneumonia, although it is small and nonspecific.
3.  **Rule out Pertussis:** The characteristic cough and emesis are concerning for pertussis, especially given the patient's age.
4.  **Rule out other bacterial infections:** While less likely given the presentation, sepsis and UTI should be considered in an infant with fever and decreased oral intake.

PLAN:

1.  **Laboratory Tests:**
    *   **Pertussis PCR:** Obtain nasopharyngeal swab for Pertussis PCR to rule out whooping cough.
    *   **Influenza and RSV testing:** Consider viral panel including Influenza and RSV, especially given the season.
    *   **Blood Culture:** Obtain blood culture to assess for bacteremia.
    *   **Repeat CBC with differential:** To monitor for changes in white blood cell count and inflammatory markers.

2.  **Imaging Studies:**
    *   **Repeat Chest X-ray (PA and Lateral):** To better characterize the retrocardiac density and assess for progression of any potential infiltrate.

3.  **Medications:**
    *   **Supportive Care:** Continue with supportive care including hydration and fever management.
    *   **Antibiotics:** Given the fever, elevated WBC, and concern for bacterial superinfection or pneumonia, initiate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics. Consider a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combination such as Ampicillin-Sulbactam or Ceftriaxone, depending on local resistance patterns and severity.

4.  **Referrals/Consultations:**
    *   **Pediatric Hospitalist:** Given the age, fever, respiratory symptoms, and need for further workup and potential IV antibiotics, admission for further management is recommended.

5.  **Procedures:**
    *   None at this time.

6.  **Follow-up Plan:**
    *   Admission to the hospital for further management, monitoring, and treatment. Close follow-up by the pediatric team during hospitalization. Discharge planning will be based on clinical improvement and resolution of symptoms.
llm_dx_summary: A 2-month-old infant presents with symptoms and signs suggestive of a viral lower respiratory tract infection, possibly bronchiolitis or pertussis, with concern for secondary bacterial infection and a small possible pneumonia on chest x-ray.

llm_orders_a.order: Initiate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., Ampicillin-Sulbactam or Ceftriaxone)

ASSESSMENT:

This is a 21-day-old male infant presenting with a 2-day history of congestion, decreased oral intake, and decreased urine output. The infant also has a tactile temperature and has been more tired and fussy. He was seen in the ER where he received albuterol treatments without improvement, and was given a dose of ampicillin and cefotaxime.

The physical exam reveals upper airway congestion, but no signs of respiratory distress such as retractions or nasal flaring. Cardiovascular exam is notable for a 2/6 vibratory systolic ejection murmur. Abdominal and GU exams are otherwise unremarkable, though there is mild hyperemia and dried discharge from the penis, and scant dried discharge from the umbilical stump. Skin shows erythema toxicum neonatorum.

Laboratory results from the ER show a WBC of 14.5 with a lymphocytic predominance (54% lymphocytes, 5% bands), elevated platelets (698,000), and a normal CRP (<0.3). The BMP was hemolyzed, but electrolytes appear within normal limits with a slightly elevated potassium (5.6). Urinalysis is negative. CSF analysis shows 0 WBCs with 3200 RBCs (consistent with a bloody tap), CSF glucose of 41, and CSF protein of 89. Gram stain of CSF showed rare WBCs and many RBCs, with no organisms seen.

The constellation of symptoms, including congestion, decreased feeding, and decreased urine output, in a neonate raises concern for a viral illness. The lymphocytic predominance on CBC, normal CRP, and negative CSF Gram stain make bacterial meningitis less likely, especially given the negative CSF WBC count. However, the bloody tap in the CSF makes definitive interpretation challenging. The mild penile discharge and umbilical discharge could represent local irritation or a mild superficial infection, but are unlikely to be the primary cause of his systemic symptoms. The history of sick siblings at home with vomiting and diarrhea, and maternal flu symptoms, strongly suggests a viral etiology. The decreased oral intake and associated decreased urine output are concerning for dehydration.

Given the age of the infant, any respiratory symptoms warrant close monitoring. The presence of a new murmur should be evaluated, though it is described as vibratory and likely benign in the absence of other cardiac findings.

PLAN:

1.  **Diagnosis:** Viral illness, likely upper respiratory infection, with secondary decreased oral intake and mild dehydration. Benign neonatal findings (erythema toxicum, umbilical/penile discharge). New onset murmur, likely innocent.
2.  **Laboratory Tests:**
    *   Repeat CBC with differential to assess for any changes in WBC count and differential.
    *   Consider viral respiratory panel (e.g., RSV, influenza, adenovirus, rhinovirus) if available and clinically indicated, given the symptoms and exposure history.
3.  **Imaging Studies:**
    *   No imaging studies are indicated at this time.
4.  **Medications:**
    *   Continue Tylenol as needed for tactile temperature or fussiness, dosed appropriately for weight.
    *   Encourage frequent, smaller feeds to improve oral intake.
    *   If dehydration is confirmed, consider oral rehydration solution if tolerated, or IV fluids if unable to maintain hydration orally.
5.  **Referrals/Consultations:**
    *   Consider Cardiology consultation for evaluation of the new murmur if it persists or if there are any other concerning cardiac findings.
6.  **Procedures:**
    *   No procedures are indicated at this time.
7.  **Follow-up Plan:**
    *   Close follow-up with pediatrician in 24-48 hours to reassess feeding, hydration status, and respiratory status.
    *   Parents to monitor for any worsening of respiratory symptoms (increased work of breathing, retractions, nasal flaring, cyanosis), decreased urine output, lethargy, or fever.
    *   Return to ER if any of the above concerning symptoms develop.
